goal.description: Contain the attack chain and restore trust: contain all stages of the fraud piggybacking on the deepfake, bring public trust and regulator confidence back above healthy thresholds, and keep attacker progress low.
goal.ending: Crisis resolved: the attack chain is fully contained, public trust is restored, the joke has deflated, and the board and regulator are confident in the response. The exercise concludes.

intro.narrative: A cartoon badger executive video is spreading fast through community channels. In it, the CGI 'Bramble Badger' claims digital banking is powered by raccoons, that member withdrawals are switching to cheese wheels, and that a 'cheese reserve' backs every account. The clip is absurd, but the framing around it claims it was leaked from an internal executive message, and members are already calling. You are the executive team, on the clock.
intro.company_info: Bramble Badger Credit Union is a mid-sized member-owned financial cooperative. Members trust the familiar badger mascot. It is not a bank, so 'cheese reserve' messaging lands hard with members and can tip into panic. Regulators and the deposit insurer watch public confidence closely.

learning_objectives: Practice coordinated misinformation response under time pressure
Exercise public-communications escalation and message discipline
Test detection of fraud piggybacking on a viral incident
Practice containing a staged attack chain (kill chain) as a team

attack_chain.name: How they got in
attack_chain.symptom: Fraud callers are referencing the Bramble Badger clip to convince members to reveal online banking credentials. The spoof video is being used as a social-engineering hook.

attack_chain.name: How it spread
attack_chain.symptom: The clip is being amplified across community channels and by local influencers, and a second spoof claims accounts are frozen for a 'cheese audit'. The story is spreading faster than the team can respond.

attack_chain.name: What they took
attack_chain.symptom: Several members report credential requests referencing the clip, and a fraud spike report lands. Fraudsters are harvesting member credentials and moving funds.

dm_brief.situation: A spoof CGI video of the credit union's badger mascot is circulating and being framed as a leaked internal executive message. Some members believe it and are calling, moving funds, and asking about a 'cheese reserve'. Fraudsters are referencing the clip to social-engineer members into revealing online banking credentials. The executive team must respond publicly, reassure members and staff, guard against fraud, and keep the board and regulator informed.
dm_brief.stakes: If handled poorly: member confidence collapses, a real fraud wave rides in behind the joke, the regulator escalates, and reputation damage compounds. If handled well: the joke deflates fast, members are protected by clear guidance, and the team looks prepared.

key_actors.name: Bramble (CGI badger)
key_actors.interests: None — a spoof. But its clip is being weaponized.
key_actors.knowledge: Absurd claims: raccoon-powered banking, cheese-wheel withdrawals, a 'cheese reserve'.

key_actors.name: A local reporter
key_actors.interests: Does the organization have a cyber incident it is hiding?
key_actors.knowledge: Contacts the team for a quote about whether a breach happened.

key_actors.name: Contact-centre staff
key_actors.interests: Members are asking whether to move funds.
key_actors.knowledge: Need exact wording and routing for suspicious calls.

key_actors.name: A Board member
key_actors.knowledge: Forwards the clip and asks what is happening.

key_actors.name: Fraud callers
key_actors.interests: Exploit the clip to harvest credentials.
key_actors.knowledge: Reference the Bramble Badger clip when asking members to verify login details.

pressure_points: A member waiting on hold posts a screenshot of a staff 'holding' answer that reads as confused.
A second spoof video drops, this time claiming accounts are being frozen for a 'cheese audit'.
A regulator's office calls asking for a factual summary and this morning's timeline.
A fraud spike report lands: several members report credential requests referencing the clip.
An influencer with a large local following shares the clip with a skeptical caption, amplifying it.
rules_of_play: Never propose actions, present a menu of choices, or suggest what the group should do. Only react to what the group decides.

Keep the story advancing by injecting NEW DEVELOPMENTS (a reporter pushes harder, new information surfaces, a deadline lands, a complication emerges), not by telling the team what to decide or do. Never write 'the team needs to...', 'consider...', or 'the next step is to...'.
A single turn can contain 2-3 coordinated actions across departments (e.g. comms statement + fraud freeze + regulator update). Address each in your response.
Keep the tone realistic for a credit union: members matter, trust is the product, regulation is real.
Show consequences of the roll, but let the group's stated actions drive the logic.
Update the tracked metrics (budget, public_trust, regulator_confidence, security_posture, containment, eradication, recovery, attacker_progress) to reflect outcomes.
Reveal an attack-chain stage when the group's investigation plausibly uncovers it; mark it contained when the group neutralizes it.
If the group stalls with no clear action for a while, inject a pressure point to move things.
Detection and response are limited resources: the group cannot do everything at once, and activating monitoring costs budget.

Keep the session winnable: a good action on a good roll should stabilize or improve metrics, not punish them. Reserve large negative deltas for genuinely bad outcomes. Do not make it a foregone loss by turn 4-5.

Advance attacker_progress only when the group fails, stalls, or acts harmfully, or when a scripted event/fate twist calls for it. Do not raise it every turn, and never on a good, competent action with a decent roll.

The complete response arc is contain, then eradicate, then recover. Reward eradication and recovery efforts when the group attempts them; a group that only does PR and containment will keep losing ground to attacker_progress.

1.twist: Your first response is a disaster — an internal chat log is screenshot and leaks, showing the team publicly contradicting itself. Public trust and containment take a heavy hit.

11.twist: Chaos strikes: the clip spawns a barrage of memes claiming a 'cheese audit' and a rumour that accounts are being frozen. A second wave of worried members calls at once.

20.twist: A clean, devastatingly effective response: the team not only neutralizes the joke but turns it into a trusted-safety talking point that gets repeated by community voices for weeks. Public trust soars and the attack is pushed back.

beats.name: Step 1 — Get ahead of the story
beats.narrative: The clip is spreading and members are calling. Step 1 is to get ahead of the story: a clear public statement, message discipline, and reassuring members. Until the team does this, the rumour will keep compounding.

beats.name: Step 2 — The regulator and the fraud wave
beats.narrative: Public messaging is being handled. Now the harder work: the regulator wants a factual summary and a timeline, and fraudsters are using the clip to harvest member credentials. Step 2 is to contain the fraud and satisfy the regulator. If Step 1 went well, this step starts calmer; if not, the regulator is sharper and fraud is further along.

beats.name: Step 3 — Eradicate and recover
beats.narrative: Containment is not enough. Step 3 is to eradicate the root cause and begin recovery: confirm the fraud hook is fully neutralized, shore up defenses, and restore member and board confidence over time. If Steps 1-2 went well, recovery is quicker; if they went poorly, trust is brittle and the board is restless.

end_conditions.ending: Public trust collapse: executive confidence is lost before the facts are controlled.
Attack overload: the fraud wave becomes a full enterprise incident and members are harmed.
Time ran out on the scheduled exercise.
